---
title: "multiple linear regression models without nonlinear effects or interaction terms"
---

Revised question: I mean multiple linear regression models without nonlinear effects or interaction terms. Can we compare models fitted using different subsets of the available predictors?

More natural academic phrasing: Compare alternative additive multiple linear regression models using different subsets of the available predictors, excluding nonlinear terms and interaction effects, and assess their out-of-sample predictive performance.

Yes. We will use ordinary multiple linear regression only, with different combinations of the six predictors: `age`, `sex`, `bmi`, `children`, `smoker`, and `region`.

Every model will have the same additive structure. No squared terms, transformations of predictors, or interaction terms will be included.

## 1. Candidate models

| Model | Predictors                                     | Purpose                                   |
| ----- | ---------------------------------------------- | ----------------------------------------- |
| M1    | All six predictors                             | Full baseline                             |
| M2    | `age + bmi + smoker`                           | Core predictors                           |
| M3    | `age + bmi + smoker + children`                | Add number of dependents                  |
| M4    | `age + bmi + smoker + sex`                     | Add sex                                   |
| M5    | `age + bmi + smoker + region`                  | Add region                                |
| M6    | `age + bmi + smoker + children + sex`          | Add dependents and sex                    |
| M7    | `age + bmi + smoker + children + region`       | Add dependents and region                 |
| M8    | `age + bmi + smoker + sex + region`            | Add sex and region                        |
| M9    | `age + bmi + children + smoker + sex + region` | Same full model as M1, written explicitly |

M1 and M9 are duplicates, so we only need one full model. We can also include reduced models to investigate how predictive performance changes when one or more predictors are omitted.

## 2. Complete R code

This code reuses your existing `insurance_train` and `insurance_test` objects to preserve the same test observations.

```
# ============================================================
# Compare additive multiple linear regression models
# No nonlinear terms and no interaction terms
# ============================================================

library(tidymodels)
library(parsnip)
library(dplyr)
library(purrr)
library(tidyr)
library(ggplot2)

# ------------------------------------------------------------
# 1. Define candidate models
# ------------------------------------------------------------

model_formulas <- list(

  M1_Full =
    charges ~ age + sex + bmi + children + smoker + region,

  M2_Core =
    charges ~ age + bmi + smoker,

  M3_Add_Children =
    charges ~ age + bmi + smoker + children,

  M4_Add_Sex =
    charges ~ age + bmi + smoker + sex,

  M5_Add_Region =
    charges ~ age + bmi + smoker + region,

  M6_Children_Sex =
    charges ~ age + bmi + smoker + children + sex,

  M7_Children_Region =
    charges ~ age + bmi + smoker + children + region,

  M8_Sex_Region =
    charges ~ age + bmi + smoker + sex + region,

  M9_Demographics =
    charges ~ age + bmi + smoker + children + sex + region,

  M10_Without_Smoker =
    charges ~ age + bmi + children + sex + region,

  M11_Age_BMI =
    charges ~ age + bmi,

  M12_BMI_Smoker =
    charges ~ bmi + smoker,

  M13_Age_Smoker =
    charges ~ age + smoker
)

# Remove duplicate formula specifications
model_formulas <- model_formulas[
  !duplicated(
    vapply(model_formulas, \(f) paste(deparse(f), collapse = ""),
           character(1))
  )
]


# ------------------------------------------------------------
# 2. Specify ordinary least squares regression
# ------------------------------------------------------------

lm_spec <- linear_reg() |>
  set_engine("lm")


# ------------------------------------------------------------
# 3. Create workflows and fit the models
# ------------------------------------------------------------

model_workflows <- purrr::map(
  model_formulas,
  \(formula) {
    workflow() |>
      add_model(lm_spec) |>
      add_formula(formula)
  }
)

fitted_models <- purrr::map(
  model_workflows,
  \(model_workflow) {
    fit(
      model_workflow,
      data = insurance_train
    )
  }
)


# ------------------------------------------------------------
# 4. Predict on the same test set
# ------------------------------------------------------------

all_predictions <- purrr::imap_dfr(
  fitted_models,
  \(model, model_name) {
    predict(
      model,
      new_data = insurance_test
    ) |>
      bind_cols(
        insurance_test |> select(charges)
      ) |>
      mutate(
        model = model_name,
        .before = 1
      )
  }
)


# ------------------------------------------------------------
# 5. Evaluate test-set performance
# ------------------------------------------------------------

evaluation_table <- all_predictions |>
  group_by(model) |>
  group_modify(
    \(data, key) {
      metric_set(rmse, mae, rsq)(
        data = data,
        truth = charges,
        estimate = .pred
      ) |>
        select(.metric, .estimate)
    }
  ) |>
  ungroup() |>
  pivot_wider(
    names_from = .metric,
    values_from = .estimate
  ) |>
  arrange(rmse)

print(evaluation_table, n = Inf)


# ------------------------------------------------------------
# 6. Compare RMSE
# ------------------------------------------------------------

ggplot(
  evaluation_table,
  aes(
    x = reorder(model, rmse),
    y = rmse
  )
) +
  geom_col() +
  coord_flip() +
  labs(
    title = "Additive Multiple Linear Regression",
    subtitle = "Test-set comparison",
    x = NULL,
    y = "RMSE"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()


# ------------------------------------------------------------
# 7. Compare MAE
# ------------------------------------------------------------

ggplot(
  evaluation_table,
  aes(
    x = reorder(model, mae),
    y = mae
  )
) +
  geom_col() +
  coord_flip() +
  labs(
    title = "Mean Absolute Error by Model",
    x = NULL,
    y = "MAE"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()


# ------------------------------------------------------------
# 8. Examine the coefficients of the best model
# ------------------------------------------------------------

best_model_name <- evaluation_table$model[1]

best_model_fit <- fitted_models[[best_model_name]]

coefficient_table <- broom::tidy(
  extract_fit_engine(best_model_fit),
  conf.int = TRUE
)

cat("Best model by test RMSE:", best_model_name, "\n")

print(coefficient_table, n = Inf)
```

## 3. How we will interpret the results

The most useful comparisons are between M1 and M2–M8.

- If M2 performs nearly as well as M1, the additional predictors may contribute little to test-set prediction accuracy.
- If removing `smoker` in M10 substantially worsens performance, smoking status is an important predictive variable.
- If M3, M4, or M5 performs better than M2, the added predictor may improve prediction.
- If M1 has the lowest RMSE, retaining all six predictors may be justified for predictive purposes.

However, a predictor can be statistically significant without materially improving out-of-sample prediction, and a small difference in RMSE does not establish that one model is genuinely better.

One important note: M1 and M9 are identical specifications, and the code removes duplicate formulas automatically. The remaining models provide a range of reduced additive specifications for comparison.

Run the code and share the resulting `evaluation_table`. We can then identify the most promising additive regression models before moving on to cross-validation or grading logic.
